problems.stem: Your prototype can log many learner events. Which logging plan best reflects data minimization tied to a stated design question?
options: Capture everything available (keystrokes, full screen video, location) in case it is useful later.
Log only the events your study question needs, such as time-on-task per item, and store them under a pseudonymous id rather than a name.
Log nothing, because any telemetry violates privacy.
Log full names alongside answers so the data is easy to read.
problems.explanation: Minimization means collecting only what a specific question requires and reducing identifiability. Capturing everything or naming learners expands risk with no design justification.

problems.stem: A teammate says, "We removed names, so the telemetry is fully anonymous." Why might this be wrong?
options: It is correct; removing names always anonymizes data.
Combining timestamps, section, and rare answer patterns can still re-identify a learner, so removing the name alone does not guarantee anonymity.
Anonymity does not matter for prototypes.
The data should not have been collected at all.
problems.explanation: De-identification is not the same as anonymization. Quasi-identifiers in combination can single out an individual even without a name.

problems.stem: You consider sending raw learner telemetry to an external AI service to summarize behavior. What is the defensible boundary?
options: Send all raw logs with identifiers, since the AI gives better summaries with more data.
Send only the minimized, pseudonymous fields your consent language covers, and confirm the service does not retain them beyond the stated purpose.
Never use any AI on learner data under any circumstance.
Send the data and decide about consent afterward if anyone asks.
problems.explanation: The boundary is set by consent scope, minimization, and retention. The tool may help, but only on data the disclosure covers and only with controlled retention.

problems.stem: Your consent form promised data only for improving the lesson. Mid-study, a colleague asks to reuse the logs for a separate marketing model. What is the principled response?
options: Share it; the data already exists, so reuse is free.
Decline or seek fresh consent, because the new purpose falls outside the boundary learners agreed to.
Share it but remove names first, which makes any reuse acceptable.
Delete all data to avoid the question.
problems.explanation: Purpose limitation binds use to what learners consented to. A new purpose requires new consent, not just de-identification.
